subject: Sunday, Nov 1 - Morning edition
body:
Spin-free news · Ranked by impact

HIGH impact NEWS daily

Morning edition · Sunday, November 1

What happened overnight, and yesterday's biggest stories. Five minutes. No spin.

Overnight

The Golden State Valkyries won the WNBA championship in only their second season, beating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 Saturday in the first Game 7 in Finals history.

Gabby Williams scored 30 points, 28 of them in the second half, and was named Finals MVP; she joined Penny Taylor (Phoenix, 2007) as the only players to score 30 or more in a winner-take-all Finals game. Golden State won the series 4-3 before 18,064 fans at Chase Center in San Francisco. Kiah Stokes had 13 rebounds and won her fourth title. For Atlanta, Jordin Canada scored 18, Allisha Gray 16, and Angel Reese had 8 points and 12 rebounds. It was Atlanta's fourth Finals loss.

Impact 4/5. A 2025 expansion team won a major U.S. pro title faster than almost any franchise in modern history. AP ↗

Trump said Saturday that "one or two" Iranian nuclear sites remain and the U.S. could hit them "in ten minutes," while Rubio said no strike decision has been made.

Speaking to reporters at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago, Trump said the U.S. is "not in that much of a hurry" because it has "knocked down their Navy" and air force, mentioned the Pickaxe Mountain site, and said talks with Iran are "going fine" but Tehran is "not very reliable." Earlier Saturday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, hosting G20 foreign ministers in Atlanta, said Trump "hasn't made a decision" on resuming strikes and prefers a diplomatic solution. The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with it, reported that Trump spoke by phone with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday; neither government has described the call.

Impact 3/5. It signals renewed U.S. strikes on Iran remain an option days before the midterms as talks stall. Fox News ↗

Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch was dismissed for good Saturday by a federal judge in Miami.

U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles dismissed the amended suit with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled, ruling that Trump did not plausibly allege the Journal acted with actual malice, the standard set by the Supreme Court's 1964 New York Times v. Sullivan decision. "Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation," Gayles wrote, calling the paper's work a "thoughtful and detailed investigation." The suit was over a July 2025 story on a sexually suggestive letter bearing Trump's name in a 2003 album for Jeffrey Epstein's 50th birthday; Trump denies writing it. Gayles first dismissed the case in April and allowed an amended complaint, filed in May. The White House did not respond to AP's request for comment; CNBC reported Trump plans to appeal.

Impact 3/5. It ends, at the trial-court level, the president's highest-profile suit against a major newspaper. AP ↗

Iran designated Britain's Royal Navy and Royal Air Force "terrorist" organizations and MI6 a "hostile group" on Sunday.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry, in a statement carried by state news agency IRNA, said the step followed a Supreme National Security Council resolution and answered Britain's July 13 move to bring Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps under its State Threats Act 2026. Tehran also accused London of joining the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran by providing bases, and said the British government bears responsibility for the consequences. No British government response had been reported by early Sunday.

Impact 2/5. It widens Iran's confrontation to a U.S. ally whose forces operate in the Gulf. Anadolu Agency ↗

A "massive" Ukrainian drone attack overnight left an industrial plant in Russia's Kstovo district with "significant damage," the regional governor said; Ukrainian media said it was a major refinery.

Nizhny Novgorod Gov. Gleb Nikitin said more than 100 drones were destroyed, there were no casualties according to preliminary information, and some homes could see temporary cuts to power, heat and hot water during repairs. He did not name the plant. Ukrainian media and war-monitoring channels identified it as Lukoil's Kstovo refinery (Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez). Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Ukraine had resumed refinery strikes after a pause, according to AFP.

Impact 2/5. Ukraine has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries after a pause. Euronews ↗

Yesterday's biggest stories

Poland's court crisis deepened Saturday as President Karol Nawrocki pushed into the Constitutional Tribunal overnight, and crisis talks ended with no plan.

Nawrocki, back from an aborted trip to Senegal, entered the tribunal around 1 a.m. Warsaw time and told judges backed by the current parliament, including Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, "You are not judges of the Constitutional Tribunal"; Korwin-Piotrowska said he barged into them, and each side blames the other for the scuffle. In a statement read outside the court, he called it a "violation of the constitutional order," demanded police withdraw and called urgent talks citing "the threat to internal security." Those talks with several parties produced no joint plan; Prime Minister Donald Tusk's Civic Coalition and the Left stayed away. In an evening address, Tusk vowed "no compromise" on the rule of law and defended the newly elected judges. Police said three protesters were arrested Friday; the court's own X account called the moves a "coup," a word Law and Justice leaders also use.

Impact 3/5. The fight over a NATO ally's top court is now a direct standoff between its president and government. AFP ↗

Trump's planned 250-foot "Triumphal Arch" faces a new lawsuit from Virginia and the District of Columbia, filed days before construction is set to begin.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb sued the National Park Service and the Interior Department in federal court in Washington on Saturday, asking for a temporary restraining order. They argue the arch at Memorial Circle, by Arlington Memorial Bridge and the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery, lacks the approval from Congress that the Commemorative Works Act requires, would break D.C.'s 130-foot height limit, and skipped environmental and historic-preservation reviews. They say three years of construction would snarl traffic between the two jurisdictions and pollute the Potomac. The administration has said work could start as early as Nov. 5. It is the third suit against the arch; U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan heard arguments Friday in the first, brought by Vietnam veterans and a historian, and said she would rule quickly.

Impact 3/5. Courts could decide within days whether the president can build a monument taller than the Statue of Liberty without Congress. AP ↗

Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, ordered the armed forces to answer any threat immediately and "without geographic limits," with U.S. and Israeli assets added to target lists.

Khamenei gave the order Saturday at a meeting with senior commanders, according to a statement on his website; he told them to update the military's target list to include U.S. and Israeli assets. Separately, Iranian state TV, citing a provincial official in Hormozgan, said U.S. forces attacked two fishing boats near Qeshm Island, wounding one fisherman; two missing men were later found. The U.S. military has not confirmed the claim, and the White House and Pentagon did not immediately respond. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called Vice President JD Vance's letter a "positive step" but said Iran has no plans to meet U.S. officials, as an Iranian team holds talks with Qatari and Pakistani mediators in Doha.

Impact 3/5. It hardens Iran's stance just as mediators try to restart U.S.-Iran talks and head off renewed war. AP ↗

Iranian strikes have damaged 274 structures at 24 bases used by U.S. forces, with repairs priced at $5 billion or more, a Wall Street Journal investigation found.

The Journal's review of satellite imagery covered installations with a U.S. presence in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE and Iraq. U.S. officials told the paper the Pentagon's internal estimate is at least $5 billion, and one assessment runs as high as $15 billion; those costs are not in the military's $47.1 billion war-cost estimate. After the July ceasefire collapsed, Iran increasingly targeted buildings housing troops, the Journal reported. The Pentagon has not publicly detailed the damage and declined to comment.

Impact 3/5. It is the fullest public accounting yet of what the war has cost U.S. bases. Wall Street Journal ↗

This week so far

The Nasdaq fell 3.4% Friday, Wall Street's worst day since June, as Intel lost about 30% in its worst day since 1974. Source ↗
Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, lost about $6.3 billion to hackers in the largest crypto theft ever; blockchain firms blame North Korea. Source ↗
The Milwaukee Brewers won the first World Series title in franchise history, beating the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 Wednesday night. Source ↗
